claim: Disruption of epithelial barriers is a common disease manifestation in chronic degenerative diseases of the airways, lung, and intestine.
source: Disruption of epithelial barriers is a common disease manifestation in chronic degenerative diseases of the airways, lung, and intestine.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific understanding of disease pathology.

claim: Extensive human genetic studies have identified risk loci in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and inflammatory bowel diseases.
source: Extensive human genetic studies have identified risk loci in such diseases, including in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and inflammatory bowel diseases.
evidence: This statement references established findings from human genetic studies, implicitly citing prior research.

claim: The screen validated the impact of candidate gene perturbations on epithelial barrier function in 56% of the cases.
source: Using intestinal barrier dysfunction in flies as a readout, our results validate the impact of candidate gene perturbations on epithelial barrier function in 56% of the cases, resulting in a prioritized target gene list.
evidence: This is a direct result from the screen described in the manuscript, supported by experimental data.

claim: nAchR signaling in enterocytes of the fly gut promotes epithelial barrier function.
source: We find that nAchR signaling in enterocytes of the fly gut promotes epithelial barrier function and epithelial homeostasis by regulating the production of the peritrophic matrix.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: nAchR signaling promotes epithelial homeostasis by regulating the production of the peritrophic matrix.
source: We find that nAchR signaling in enterocytes of the fly gut promotes epithelial barrier function and epithelial homeostasis by regulating the production of the peritrophic matrix.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Loss of intestinal barrier function in Drosophila is accompanied by commensal dysbiosis and inflammation.
source: In Drosophila, loss of intestinal barrier function is accompanied by commensal dysbiosis and inflammation and reliably predicts impending organismal death (Rera et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rera et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of intestinal barrier function in Drosophila reliably predicts impending organismal death.
source: In Drosophila, loss of intestinal barrier function is accompanied by commensal dysbiosis and inflammation and reliably predicts impending organismal death (Rera et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rera et al., 2012.

claim: Increased barrier permeability has been reported in inflammatory bowel disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
source: Similarly, increased barrier permeability and changes in microbiome composition and abundance have been reported in various human diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Raftery et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raftery et al., 2020.

claim: Changes in microbiome composition and abundance have been reported in inflammatory bowel disease and COPD.
source: Similarly, increased barrier permeability and changes in microbiome composition and abundance have been reported in various human diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Raftery et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Raftery et al., 2020.

claim: COPD is a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality.
source: COPD is a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality and is characterized by an obstructed airflow resulting in shortness of breath upon exertion.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about COPD.

claim: COPD is characterized by an obstructed airflow resulting in shortness of breath upon exertion.
source: COPD is a major contributor to global morbidity and mortality and is characterized by an obstructed airflow resulting in shortness of breath upon exertion.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about COPD symptoms.

claim: Lungs of COPD patients display chronic inflammation, extensive cellular remodeling, and barrier dysfunction.
source: At the tissue level, lungs of COPD patients display chronic inflammation, extensive cellular remodeling, and barrier dysfunction (Aghapour et al., 2018; Barnes, 2019; Carlier et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aghapour et al., 2018; Barnes, 2019; Carlier et al., 2021.

claim: Many COPD patients are non-smokers, suggesting a genetic component contributing to disease susceptibility.
source: While smoking or exposure to environmental air pollutants remain major risk factors, many COPD patients are non-smokers, suggesting a genetic component contributing to disease susceptibility (Aghapour et al., 2022; Barnes, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Aghapour et al., 2022; Barnes, 2019.

claim: Several genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified risk loci for incidence of COPD.
source: Several genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have been performed in which risk loci for incidence of COPD have been identified (Hobbs et al., 2017; Pillai et al., 2009; Sakornsakolpat et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hobbs et al., 2017; Pillai et al., 2009; Sakornsakolpat et al., 2019.

claim: One of the most well-known COPD risk loci is located near the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) CHRNA3/5 genes.
source: One of the most well-known risk loci is located near the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) CHRNA3/5 genes and has also been associated with increased nicotine dependence and smoking behavior, and lung cancer (Amos et al., 2008; Carlier et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2014; Hobbs et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2008; Pillai et al., 2009; Wilk et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The CHRNA3/5 risk locus has been associated with increased nicotine dependence and smoking behavior, and lung cancer.
source: One of the most well-known risk loci is located near the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAchR) CHRNA3/5 genes and has also been associated with increased nicotine dependence and smoking behavior, and lung cancer (Amos et al., 2008; Carlier et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2014; Hobbs et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2008; Pillai et al., 2009; Wilk et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Amos et al., 2008; Carlier et al., 2021; Cui et al., 2014; Hobbs et al., 2017; Hung et al., 2008; Pillai et al., 2009; Wilk et al., 2012.

claim: CHRNA5 plays a role in the formation of COPD-like lesions in the respiratory epithelium independently of cigarette smoke.
source: Recent work has demonstrated a role for CHRNA5 in the formation of COPD-like lesions in the respiratory epithelium independently of cigarette smoke, suggesting a direct involvement of nAchRs in shaping epithelial integrity (Routhier et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Routhier et al., 2021.

claim: Acetylcholine (Ach) is synthesized by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) in cholinergic neurons, immune cells, and epithelial cells such as brush/tuft cells.
source: The endogenous ligand of nAchR, acetylcholine (Ach), is a classic neurotransmitter synthesized by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) in cholinergic neurons, as well as in immune cells and epithelial cells, such as brush/tuft cells (Kummer and Krasteva-Christ, 2014; Wessler and Kirkpatrick, 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kummer and Krasteva-Christ, 2014; Wessler and Kirkpatrick, 2008.

claim: Brush/tuft cells orchestrate type 2 inflammatory responses.
source: Such cells orchestrate type 2 inflammatory responses (Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021), mucociliary clearance (Perniss et al., 2020), and limit biliary inflammation (O'Leary et al., 2022; O'Leary et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021.

claim: Brush/tuft cells regulate mucociliary clearance.
source: Such cells orchestrate type 2 inflammatory responses (Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021), mucociliary clearance (Perniss et al., 2020), and limit biliary inflammation (O'Leary et al., 2022; O'Leary et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Perniss et al., 2020.

claim: Brush/tuft cells limit biliary inflammation.
source: Such cells orchestrate type 2 inflammatory responses (Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021), mucociliary clearance (Perniss et al., 2020), and limit biliary inflammation (O'Leary et al., 2022; O'Leary et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to O'Leary et al., 2022; O'Leary et al., 2019.

claim: The Drosophila intestine is lined by a pseudostratified epithelium consisting of enterocytes (ECs) and enteroendocrine cells (EEs) that are regenerated from a basal population of intestinal stem cells (ISCs).
source: The Drosophila intestine is lined by a pseudostratified epithelium consisting of enterocytes (ECs) and enteroendocrine cells (EEs) that are regenerated from a basal population of intestinal stem cells (ISCs) (Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Miguel-Aliaga et al., 2018.

claim: The fly intestinal epithelium resembles mammalian airway epithelia in its structure, cell composition and molecular regulation of regenerative processes.
source: In its structure, cell composition and molecular regulation of regenerative processes, the fly intestinal epithelium resembles mammalian airway epithelia (Biteau et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Biteau et al., 2011.

claim: Under stress conditions, in response to enteropathogen infection, and during normal aging, the fly intestinal epithelium loses its barrier function and exhibits stem cell hyperplasia and commensal dysbiosis.
source: Under stress conditions, in response to enteropathogen infection, as well as during normal aging, the fly intestinal epithelium loses its barrier function and exhibits stem cell hyperplasia and commensal dysbiosis (Jasper, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jasper, 2020.

claim: The phenotypes observed in the fly intestinal epithelium recapitulate changes observed in airway epithelia of COPD patients.
source: These phenotypes recapitulate changes observed in airway epithelia of COPD patients and can thus be used as a model for pathophysiological changes occurring in this disease (Carlier et al., 2021; Raftery et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Carlier et al., 2021; Raftery et al., 2020.

claim: Several of the candidate genes identified in the screen as required for barrier integrity encode for subunits of the nAchR.
source: Several of the candidate genes identified in this screen as required for barrier integrity encode for subunits of the nAchR.
evidence: This is a direct result from the screen described in the manuscript.

claim: ChAT is expressed by a subset of EEs in the fly intestine.
source: In the fly intestine, we find that ChAT is expressed by a subset of EEs and that EC-specific expression of nAchR is required for barrier integrity by stimulating chitin release and ensuring maintenance of the peritrophic matrix (PM), a chitinous structure protecting the epithelium from luminal insults.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: EC-specific expression of nAchR is required for barrier integrity by stimulating chitin release and ensuring maintenance of the peritrophic matrix (PM).
source: In the fly intestine, we find that ChAT is expressed by a subset of EEs and that EC-specific expression of nAchR is required for barrier integrity by stimulating chitin release and ensuring maintenance of the peritrophic matrix (PM), a chitinous structure protecting the epithelium from luminal insults.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The peritrophic matrix (PM) is a chitinous structure protecting the epithelium from luminal insults.
source: In the fly intestine, we find that ChAT is expressed by a subset of EEs and that EC-specific expression of nAchR is required for barrier integrity by stimulating chitin release and ensuring maintenance of the peritrophic matrix (PM), a chitinous structure protecting the epithelium from luminal insults.
evidence: This is a description of the PM based on established knowledge.

claim: Ach is required for the expression of Syt4 in ECs.
source: In ECs, Ach is required for the expression of Syt4, a critical regulator of exocytosis (Yoshihara et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011) which is required for the maintenance of PM structure and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Syt4 is a critical regulator of exocytosis.
source: In ECs, Ach is required for the expression of Syt4, a critical regulator of exocytosis (Yoshihara et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011) which is required for the maintenance of PM structure and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Yoshihara et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011.

claim: Syt4 is required for the maintenance of PM structure and epithelial barrier function.
source: In ECs, Ach is required for the expression of Syt4, a critical regulator of exocytosis (Yoshihara et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2011) which is required for the maintenance of PM structure and epithelial barrier function.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of various nAchR subunits with da-GS leads to mild barrier dysfunction under homeostatic conditions.
source: Ubiquitous knockdown of various nAchR subunits with da-GS lead to mild barrier dysfunction under homeostatic conditions, and greatly enhanced barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a sensitization of the epithelium to stress.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ubiquitous knockdown of various nAchR subunits with da-GS greatly enhances barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge.
source: Ubiquitous knockdown of various nAchR subunits with da-GS lead to mild barrier dysfunction under homeostatic conditions, and greatly enhanced barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a sensitization of the epithelium to stress.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR subunits sensitizes the epithelium to stress.
source: Ubiquitous knockdown of various nAchR subunits with da-GS lead to mild barrier dysfunction under homeostatic conditions, and greatly enhanced barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), suggesting a sensitization of the epithelium to stress.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference from the observed results.

claim: Modulation of total organismal Ach levels by RNAi-mediated silencing of ChAT results in increased barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure.
source: Modulation of total organismal Ach levels by RNAi-mediated silencing of ChAT under control of da-GS also resulted in increased barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), further supporting the role of Ach/nAChR signaling in maintaining intestinal epithelial homeostasis.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR α4 or β3 with NP1ts or 5966-GS increases the numbers of smurf flies, indicating a defective epithelial barrier.
source: Knockdown of nAchR α4 or β3 with both drivers increased the numbers of smurf flies, indicating a defective epithelial barrier (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs results in induction of ISC proliferation.
source: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs resulted in various hallmarks of epithelial stress. These include induction of ISC proliferation (Figure 2E), presumably due to stress signals released by ECs (Biteau et al., 2011), as well as activation of JAK/STAT signaling (measured using the 2xSTAT::GFP reporter; Bach et al., 2007) and ER stress signaling (measured using an Xbp1-eGFP reporter; Sone et al., 2013; Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ISC proliferation after nAchR knockdown in ECs is presumably due to stress signals released by ECs.
source: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs resulted in various hallmarks of epithelial stress. These include induction of ISC proliferation (Figure 2E), presumably due to stress signals released by ECs (Biteau et al., 2011), as well as activation of JAK/STAT signaling (measured using the 2xSTAT::GFP reporter; Bach et al., 2007) and ER stress signaling (measured using an Xbp1-eGFP reporter; Sone et al., 2013; Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by a citation to Biteau et al., 2011.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs results in activation of JAK/STAT signaling.
source: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs resulted in various hallmarks of epithelial stress. These include induction of ISC proliferation (Figure 2E), presumably due to stress signals released by ECs (Biteau et al., 2011), as well as activation of JAK/STAT signaling (measured using the 2xSTAT::GFP reporter; Bach et al., 2007) and ER stress signaling (measured using an Xbp1-eGFP reporter; Sone et al., 2013; Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs results in activation of ER stress signaling.
source: Knockdown of nAchR in ECs resulted in various hallmarks of epithelial stress. These include induction of ISC proliferation (Figure 2E), presumably due to stress signals released by ECs (Biteau et al., 2011), as well as activation of JAK/STAT signaling (measured using the 2xSTAT::GFP reporter; Bach et al., 2007) and ER stress signaling (measured using an Xbp1-eGFP reporter; Sone et al., 2013; Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Organization of epithelial junctions in ECs remains mostly unaltered after nAchR knockdown.
source: Interestingly, organization of epithelial junctions in ECs remained mostly unaltered, as visualized by staining for the septate junction marker Dlg and Coracle as well as localization of arm-GFP, suggesting that barrier dysfunction may be caused by a separate mechanism (Figure 2H and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H, I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Barrier dysfunction after nAchR knockdown may be caused by a mechanism separate from junctional disruption.
source: Interestingly, organization of epithelial junctions in ECs remained mostly unaltered, as visualized by staining for the septate junction marker Dlg and Coracle as well as localization of arm-GFP, suggesting that barrier dysfunction may be caused by a separate mechanism (Figure 2H and I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that junctions remain intact despite barrier dysfunction.

claim: Individual knockdown of nAchR α2, α4, β1, or β3 in stem cells results in increased barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge.
source: Individual knockdown of nAchR α2, α4, β1, or β3 resulted in increased barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge as well as decreased survival after P. entomophila (PE) infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Individual knockdown of nAchR α2, α4, β1, or β3 in stem cells results in decreased survival after P. entomophila (PE) infection.
source: Individual knockdown of nAchR α2, α4, β1, or β3 resulted in increased barrier dysfunction after Paraquat challenge as well as decreased survival after P. entomophila (PE) infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: Stem cells depleted for various nAchR subunits undergo mitosis at a similar rate as control counterparts when challenged with PE.
source: When challenged with PE, stem cells depleted for various nAchR subunits underwent mitosis at a similar rate as their control counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that barrier dysfunction is not caused by an inability of stem cells to regenerate the epithelium.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Barrier dysfunction after nAchR knockdown in stem cells is not caused by an inability of stem cells to regenerate the epithelium.
source: When challenged with PE, stem cells depleted for various nAchR subunits underwent mitosis at a similar rate as their control counterparts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that barrier dysfunction is not caused by an inability of stem cells to regenerate the epithelium.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that stem cell proliferation is not affected.

claim: Only 32% of nAChR α2 clones contained at least 1 EE compared to 72% of clones in the control samples.
source: Interestingly, however, they failed to produce normal numbers of EEs, as only 32% of nAChR α2 clones contained at least 1 EE compared to 72% of clones in the control samples (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: nAChR α2 clones fail to produce normal numbers of EEs.
source: Interestingly, however, they failed to produce normal numbers of EEs, as only 32% of nAChR α2 clones contained at least 1 EE compared to 72% of clones in the control samples (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: nAchR may be required for the proper differentiation of EEs.
source: In addition to a broader role for nAchR in maintaining barrier integrity, nAchR may thus also be required for the proper differentiation of EEs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that nAChR mutant clones have fewer EEs.

claim: Expression of UAS-GFP under the control of two independently established ChAT-Gal4 drivers confirms that some enteric neurons are cholinergic.
source: Expression of UAS-GFP under the control of two independently established ChAT-Gal4 drivers confirmed that some of these neurons are indeed cholinergic (Figure 3A and B', Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B' and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A subset of prospero-positive EEs express GFP under ChAT-Gal4 control, predominantly located in the R4 and R5 regions of the midgut.
source: Upon closer examination of the epithelium, we also noticed a subset of prospero-positive EEs expressing GFP, predominantly located in the R4 and R5 regions of the midgut (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ChAT antibody staining labels more cells than ChAT-Gal4, suggesting that this driver may not fully capture all EEs expressing ChAT.
source: ChAT antibody staining labeled more cells than ChAT-Gal4 (Mi{Trojan-GAL4.0}ChAT[MI04508-TG4.0] CG7715[MI04508-TG4.0-X]), suggesting that this driver may not fully capture all EEs expressing ChAT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of antibody staining and driver expression patterns.

claim: Depletion of nAchR subunits in ECs does not affect the number of EEs.
source: Depletion of nAchR subunits in ECs did not affect the number of EEs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Depletion of ChAT in EEs with prosts renders flies more susceptible to barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure.
source: Reduction of ChAT levels with both drivers rendered flies more susceptible to barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Depletion of ChAT with ChATts renders flies more susceptible to barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure.
source: Reduction of ChAT levels with both drivers rendered flies more susceptible to barrier dysfunction after Paraquat exposure (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Ach-mediated crosstalk between cholinergic neurons and/or EEs with ECs is critical to maintain intestinal epithelial homeostasis.
source: Since depletion of several nAchR subunits in ECs, or of ChAT in neurons and EEs leads to loss of barrier integrity and decreased survival after chemical or bacterial challenge, we propose that Ach-mediated crosstalk between cholinergic neurons and/or EEs with ECs is critical to maintain intestinal epithelial homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: PCA analysis shows that transcriptomes from intestines with nAchR knockdown are clearly distinct from transcriptomes of intestines with a control RNAi construct.
source: PCA suggested that the transcriptomes from intestines with nAchR knockdown were clearly distinct from transcriptomes of intestines with a control RNAi construct (mCherry RNAi; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: 240 genes were upregulated and 215 genes were downregulated after nAchR knockdown in ECs.
source: Overall, we observed 240 upregulated and 215 downregulated genes (Figure 4B; FDR ≤ 0.1; log2(fold change) <–1 or >1; 100% of samples have ≥1 reads), of which 171 were differentially expressed in both nAchR β1 and β3 knockdowns, supporting the idea that these subunits have partially overlapping functions (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 171 genes were differentially expressed in both nAchR β1 and β3 knockdowns, supporting the idea that these subunits have partially overlapping functions.
source: Overall, we observed 240 upregulated and 215 downregulated genes (Figure 4B; FDR ≤ 0.1; log2(fold change) <–1 or >1; 100% of samples have ≥1 reads), of which 171 were differentially expressed in both nAchR β1 and β3 knockdowns, supporting the idea that these subunits have partially overlapping functions (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of differentially expressed genes between the two knockdowns.

claim: Synaptotagmin 4 (Syt4) was the most significantly downregulated gene in both nAchR β1 and β3 knockdowns.
source: Synaptotagmin 4 (Syt4) was the most significantly downregulated gene in both knockdowns (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis revealed increased expression of glucosidases and hydrolases after nAchR knockdown.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis revealed increased expression of glucosidases and hydrolases after nAchR knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F), and downregulation of genes involved in immune responses such as lysozymes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and genes related to chitin binding and metabolism (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis revealed downregulation of genes involved in immune responses such as lysozymes after nAchR knockdown.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis revealed increased expression of glucosidases and hydrolases after nAchR knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F), and downregulation of genes involved in immune responses such as lysozymes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and genes related to chitin binding and metabolism (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: GO term enrichment analysis revealed downregulation of genes related to chitin binding and metabolism after nAchR knockdown.
source: Gene ontology (GO) term enrichment analysis revealed increased expression of glucosidases and hydrolases after nAchR knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, F), and downregulation of genes involved in immune responses such as lysozymes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and genes related to chitin binding and metabolism (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Syt4 was the most significantly downregulated gene after ChAT depletion in EEs.
source: However, Syt4 remained the most significantly downregulated gene (Figure 4H) and enriched GO terms overlapped significantly with the previous experiment, especially with regard to immune responses (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Chitin-related GO terms were trending towards enrichment among downregulated genes after ChAT depletion in EEs.
source: Chitin-related GO terms were also trending towards enrichment among downregulated genes (Figure 4G), and the genes associated with these terms partially overlapped with the ones identified after nAchR knockdown (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: 56 genes overlap between guts depleted for nAchR in ECs and guts where ChAT was silenced using prosts.
source: Direct comparison of differentially regulated genes revealed an overlap of 56 genes between guts depleted for nAchR in ECs and guts where ChAT was silenced using prosts (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison of RNAseq data sets shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The enrichment of chitin GO terms in RNAseq experiments prompted examination of the PM.
source: The enrichment of chitin GO terms in our RNAseq experiments prompted us to examine the PM.
evidence: This is a statement of the rationale for subsequent experiments based on the RNAseq findings.

claim: The PM is a protective structure lining the gut of many insects, consisting of crosslinked glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and chitin.
source: The PM is a protective structure lining the gut of many insects, consisting of crosslinked glycoproteins, proteoglycans, and chitin (Erlandson et al., 2019; Hegedus et al., 2009; Hegedus et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Erlandson et al., 2019; Hegedus et al., 2009; Hegedus et al., 2019.

claim: The PM surrounds the food bolus and forms a selectively permeable physical barrier preventing direct contact between abrasive food particles and bacteria with the epithelium.
source: It surrounds the food bolus and forms a selectively permeable physical barrier preventing direct contact between abrasive food particles and bacteria with the epithelium, thus helping to compartmentalize digestive processes as well as protecting the animal from ingested toxins and pathogens (Erlandson et al., 2019; Hegedus et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Erlandson et al., 2019; Hegedus et al., 2019.

claim: The PM protects against pathogenic bacteria and their pore-forming toxins, such as Pseudomonas entomophilia and Serratia marcescens.
source: In flies, it was shown that the PM protects against pathogenic bacteria and their pore-forming toxins, such as Pseudomonas entomophilia and Serratia marcescens (Kuraishi et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kuraishi et al., 2011.

claim: Dipteran insects such as Drosophila continuously produce a type II PM originating in the cardia at the anterior end of the midgut.
source: Dipteran insects such as Drosophila are thought to continuously produce a type II PM originating in the cardia at the anterior end of the midgut (Hegedus et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hegedus et al., 2019.

claim: There is evidence suggesting remodeling activity along the posterior midgut, as transcripts for PM components were found enriched in the R4 region of the midgut.
source: There is evidence suggesting remodeling activity along the posterior midgut, as transcripts for PM components were found enriched in the R4 region of the midgut (Buchon et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Buchon et al., 2013.

claim: Intestinal IMD signaling and a subset of enteric neurons have been implicated in modulating the composition and permeability of the PM.
source: Moreover, intestinal IMD signaling as well as a subset of enteric neurons have been implicated in modulating the composition and permeability of the PM, however the underlying molecular mechanisms of PM remodeling remain poorly understood (Buchon et al., 2009b; Kenmoku et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Buchon et al., 2009b; Kenmoku et al., 2016.

claim: Transcript levels of CG32302, a putative component of the PM, were noticeably reduced in guts depleted of nAchR subunits.
source: Transcript levels of a putative component of the PM, CG32302, were noticeably reduced in guts depleted of nAchR subunits (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Depletion of nAchR subunits in ECs significantly reduces survival after PE infection.
source: Indeed, depletion of nAchR subunits in ECs significantly reduced survival after PE infection (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Overnight (16 hr) PE infection leads to a significant upregulation of nAchR β3 subunit transcript levels.
source: Overnight (16 hr) PE infection led to a significant upregulation of nAchR β3 subunit transcript levels, while Ace levels were significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a possible activation of the pathway in response to infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Overnight (16 hr) PE infection leads to a significant reduction of Ace levels.
source: Overnight (16 hr) PE infection led to a significant upregulation of nAchR β3 subunit transcript levels, while Ace levels were significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a possible activation of the pathway in response to infection.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Changes in nAchR β3 and Ace transcript levels after PE infection indicate a possible activation of the pathway in response to infection.
source: Overnight (16 hr) PE infection led to a significant upregulation of nAchR β3 subunit transcript levels, while Ace levels were significantly reduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating a possible activation of the pathway in response to infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in transcript levels.

claim: ChAT transcript levels remain unaffected by pathogenic infection.
source: ChAT transcript levels as well as numbers of ChAT-expressing cells in the gut epithelium remained unaffected by pathogenic infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Numbers of ChAT-expressing cells in the gut epithelium remain unaffected by pathogenic infection.
source: ChAT transcript levels as well as numbers of ChAT-expressing cells in the gut epithelium remained unaffected by pathogenic infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: Silencing of nAchR β1 or β3 leads to spiny protrusions of the fluorescent matter in the bead feeding assay, indicating a damaged PM.
source: The surface of the bead-containing ingested food appeared relatively smooth in control animals. In contrast, silencing of nAchR β1 or β3 led to spiny protrusions of the fluorescent matter, indicating a damaged PM (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Guts depleted of nAchR α4 display fluorescent signal scattered throughout the lumen and making contact with the brush border.
source: Guts depleted of nAchR α4 displayed fluorescent signal scattered throughout the lumen and making contact with the brush border while the beads stayed confined to the PM sleeve and separated from the epithelium in control guts (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In 56% of nAchR β1 knockdown samples, the thin PM layer was clearly disrupted or missing altogether.
source: However, in 56% of samples the thin layer was clearly disrupted or missing altogether (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In all examined control and knockdown guts, the septate junctions connecting adjacent cells appeared normal.
source: In all examined control and knockdown guts, the septate junctions connecting adjacent cells appeared normal, consistent with our Dlg and coracle staining (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), as well as the fact that no changes in junctional protein expression was observed in our RNAseq experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the electron microscopy analysis consistent with previous immunofluorescence and RNAseq data.

claim: The amount of CFUs after 8 days of nAchR β1, β3, or α4 silencing exceeds control levels significantly, indicating that these flies struggle to maintain appropriate commensal numbers.
source: The amount of CFUs after 8 days of nAchR β1, β3, or α4 silencing exceeded control levels significantly, indicating that these flies struggle to maintain appropriate commensal numbers (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Reduction of nAchR levels leads to an increase of disturbed acidity patterns in the gut.
source: Reduction of nAchR levels lead to an increase of disturbed acidity patterns, ranging from completely blue guts to samples with weak staining and white patches, which has been attributed to expansion of acid-producing commensals like Lactobacillus along the whole gut (Li et al., 2016; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Depletion of ChAT in EEs with prosts causes increased susceptibility to PE infection.
source: Furthermore, depletion of ChAT in EEs with prosts also caused increased susceptibility to PE infection (Figure 5F) as well as dysbiosis (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Depletion of ChAT in EEs with prosts causes dysbiosis.
source: Furthermore, depletion of ChAT in EEs with prosts also caused increased susceptibility to PE infection (Figure 5F) as well as dysbiosis (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Overexpression of ChAT promotes survival after bacterial infection.
source: Conversely, overexpression of ChAT promoted survival after bacterial infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ach signaling is required to maintain a healthy microbiome and protect the animals against pathogenic infections.
source: Together these results suggest that Ach signaling is required to maintain a healthy microbiome and protect the animals against pathogenic infections.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on dysbiosis and infection susceptibility.

claim: Synaptotagmin 4 is a vesicular Ca2+-binding protein promoting retrograde signaling at synapses.
source: One of the most significantly downregulated genes identified in our RNAseq data sets is Synaptotagmin 4, a vesicular Ca2+-binding protein promoting retrograde signaling at synapses (Yoshihara et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Yoshihara et al., 2005.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of Syt4 under control of NP1ts reduces survival after challenge with PE.
source: RNAi-meditated silencing of Syt4 under control of NP1ts reduced survival after challenge with PE (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and caused PM defects visualized with the bead feeding assay (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi-mediated silencing of Syt4 causes PM defects visualized with the bead feeding assay.
source: RNAi-meditated silencing of Syt4 under control of NP1ts reduced survival after challenge with PE (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A) and caused PM defects visualized with the bead feeding assay (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Syt4 depletion increases commensal numbers.
source: Moreover, Syt4 depletion increased commensal numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), disrupted gut compartmentalization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as well as the morphology of the gastric region: Acid-producing copper cells usually form deep invaginations of the apical membrane (Dubreuil, 2004), giving rise to a gastric unit that can be visualized with anti-cut staining (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Syt4 depletion disrupts gut compartmentalization.
source: Moreover, Syt4 depletion increased commensal numbers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), disrupted gut compartmentalization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), as well as the morphology of the gastric region: Acid-producing copper cells usually form deep invaginations of the apical membrane (Dubreuil, 2004), giving rise to a gastric unit that can be visualized with anti-cut staining (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Syt4 depletion results in a disorganized morphology and a marked flattening of gastric units.
source: Syt4 depletion resulted in a disorganized morphology and a marked flattening of these units (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Combined knockdown of Syt4 and nAchR subunits does not have an additive effect on survival after PE infection, consistent with an epistatic relationship between these genes.
source: Combined knockdown of Syt4 and nAchR subunits did not have an additive effect on survival after PE infection, consistent with an epistatic relationship between these genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, suggesting an epistatic relationship.

claim: Syt4 null mutant animals display enhanced susceptibility to PE challenge.
source: While these mutant animals were homozygous viable, they displayed enhanced susceptibility to PE challenge (Figure 6C) and a fragmented PM, often accompanied by enlarged WGA-positive structures within the epithelium (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Syt4 null mutant animals display a fragmented PM, often accompanied by enlarged WGA-positive structures within the epithelium.
source: While these mutant animals were homozygous viable, they displayed enhanced susceptibility to PE challenge (Figure 6C) and a fragmented PM, often accompanied by enlarged WGA-positive structures within the epithelium (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Overexpression of 3xFLAG-mCherry-Syt4 with NP1ts has a protective effect on animal survival after PE challenge.
source: Overexpression of this construct with NP1ts had a protective effect on animal survival after PE challenge (Figure 6E), but was not able to rescue PE sensitivity when nAchR subunits were knocked down simultaneously, suggesting that Syt4 expression is not sufficient for barrier protection in an nAchR loss of function context (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Overexpression of Syt4 is not able to rescue PE sensitivity when nAchR subunits are knocked down simultaneously, suggesting that Syt4 expression is not sufficient for barrier protection in an nAchR loss of function context.
source: Overexpression of this construct with NP1ts had a protective effect on animal survival after PE challenge (Figure 6E), but was not able to rescue PE sensitivity when nAchR subunits were knocked down simultaneously, suggesting that Syt4 expression is not sufficient for barrier protection in an nAchR loss of function context (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I, leading to an inference about the relationship between Syt4 and nAchR.

claim: There is a significant colocalization of Syt4-mCherry-positive structures and WGA staining in immunofluorescence experiments, suggesting that Syt4 vesicles contain chitin.
source: Interestingly, we noticed a significant colocalization of Syt4-mCherry-positive structures and WGA staining in immunofluorescence experiments, suggesting that Syt4 vesicles contain chitin (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F, leading to an inference about the content of Syt4 vesicles.

claim: Immunogold electron microscopy confirms the colocalization of mCherry-Syt4 and WGA in vesicular structures containing highly folded membrane swirls and amorphous cargo.
source: Immunogold electron microscopy confirmed the colocalization of mCherry-Syt4 and WGA in vesicular structures containing highly folded membrane swirls and amorphous cargo (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The study identified 22 candidate COPD genes that modulate barrier integrity in the fly.
source: Our study identified 22 candidate COPD genes that modulate barrier integrity in the fly and demonstrate the utility of the genetically accessible fly to screen candidate disease genes from human GWAS to provide mechanistic insight into their role in tissue homeostasis and pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The study demonstrates the utility of the genetically accessible fly to screen candidate disease genes from human GWAS to provide mechanistic insight into their role in tissue homeostasis and pathophysiology.
source: Our study identified 22 candidate COPD genes that modulate barrier integrity in the fly and demonstrate the utility of the genetically accessible fly to screen candidate disease genes from human GWAS to provide mechanistic insight into their role in tissue homeostasis and pathophysiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the approach used in the study.

claim: The role of nAchR signaling is mediated by transcriptional regulation of Syt4 in ECs, which in turn maintains secretion of chitin vesicles to maintain the PM.
source: This role of nAchR signaling is mediated by transcriptional regulation of Syt4 in ECs, which in turn maintains secretion of chitin vesicles to maintain the PM (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the experimental data, illustrated in Figure 6H.

claim: Neuronal Ach seems to be the main driver regulating return to homeostasis after injury.
source: Recent work suggests a vital role of neuronally derived Ach during regeneration (Petsakou et al., 2023). While neuronal Ach seems to be the main driver regulating return to homeostasis after injury, it is possible that Ach secreted by both cell types may contribute to the maintenance of the epithelium under homeostatic conditions and it will be of interest to explore these contributions in future studies.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Petsakou et al., 2023.

claim: It is possible that Ach secreted by both neurons and EEs may contribute to the maintenance of the epithelium under homeostatic conditions.
source: Recent work suggests a vital role of neuronally derived Ach during regeneration (Petsakou et al., 2023). While neuronal Ach seems to be the main driver regulating return to homeostasis after injury, it is possible that Ach secreted by both cell types may contribute to the maintenance of the epithelium under homeostatic conditions and it will be of interest to explore these contributions in future studies.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible contributions of different Ach sources.

claim: nAchR β3 is induced and Ace is repressed after PE infection, suggesting that the pathway is dynamically regulated in response to enteropathogen infection.
source: Our transcriptome analysis, which shows that nAchR β3 is induced and Ace is repressed after PE infection, is in line with previous findings and suggests that the pathway is dynamically regulated in response to enteropathogen infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the transcriptome analysis data.

claim: Ca2+ signaling in ECs may strengthen PM integrity through promoting Syt4-mediated vesicle fusion.
source: In addition to regulating tissue recovery, Ca2+ signaling in ECs may also strengthen PM integrity through promoting Syt4-mediated vesicle fusion (Wang and Chapman, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to Wang and Chapman, 2010.

claim: nAchR signaling only mildly impacts regenerative processes, influencing the balance between EEs and ECs in newly formed cell populations.
source: Our data using nAChR subunit loss of function clones suggest that nAchR signaling only mildly impacts regenerative processes, influencing the balance between EEs and ECs in newly formed cell populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MARCM clone data.

claim: A role for Ach signaling in human barrier epithelia is supported by previous studies showing that muscarinic Ach receptors have been successfully targeted in the clinic to relieve bronchoconstriction and mucus hypersecretion in COPD and asthma.
source: A role for Ach signaling in human barrier epithelia is supported by previous studies: muscarinic Ach receptors have been successfully targeted in the clinic to relieve bronchoconstriction and mucus hypersecretion in COPD and asthma (Calzetta et al., 2021), although nicotinic AchRs remain more elusive from a therapeutic perspective (Hollenhorst and Krasteva-Christ, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Calzetta et al., 2021 and Hollenhorst and Krasteva-Christ, 2021.

claim: Airway tuft cells have been implicated in orchestrating type 2 inflammatory responses and mucociliary clearance.
source: Airway tuft cells have been implicated in orchestrating type 2 inflammatory responses (Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021) and mucociliary clearance (Perniss et al., 2020), whereas their intestinal counterparts participate in defense against helminths and protists and limit biliary inflammation (O'Leary et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021; Perniss et al., 2020.

claim: Intestinal tuft cells participate in defense against helminths and protists and limit biliary inflammation.
source: Airway tuft cells have been implicated in orchestrating type 2 inflammatory responses (Parker et al., 2019; Sell et al., 2021) and mucociliary clearance (Perniss et al., 2020), whereas their intestinal counterparts participate in defense against helminths and protists and limit biliary inflammation (O'Leary et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to O'Leary et al., 2019; Parker et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of a COPD risk allele of CHRNA5 in epithelial cells leads to airway remodeling in vivo, increased proliferation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines through decreased calcium entry and increased adenylyl-cyclase activity.
source: Accordingly, it was recently reported that expression of a COPD risk allele of CHRNA5 in epithelial cells leads to airway remodeling in vivo, increased proliferation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines through decreased calcium entry and increased adenylyl-cyclase activity (Routhier et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Routhier et al., 2021.

claim: Previous work has shown a downregulation of junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and p120 after depletion of CHRNA5 in A549 lung cancer cells.
source: Previous work has further shown a downregulation of junctional proteins such as ZO-1 and p120 after depletion of CHRNA5 in A549 lung cancer cells (Krais et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Krais et al., 2011.

claim: The Drosophila PM is functionally analogous to mucus and surfactant layers in mammalian airways.
source: Our study highlights the evolutionary conservation of mechanisms maintaining epithelial barrier function. The PM is functionally analogous to mucus and surfactant layers in mammalian airways, and it remains to be explored whether COPD risk alleles in nAchR subunits also cause a dysfunction in the secretion of such barrier components.
evidence: This is a statement about functional analogy based on established knowledge.

claim: The epithelial dysfunction observed in mice expressing the CHRNA5 risk allele emerges independently of cigarette smoke.
source: It is critical to note that the epithelial dysfunction observed in these animals, as well as part of the association of COPD risk with specific CHRNA loci, emerges independently of cigarette smoke (Parker et al., 2019; Routhier et al., 2021; Siedlinski et al., 2013), indicating that nAchR signaling is critical to maintain homeostasis not only in the context of oxidative stress, but under homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Parker et al., 2019; Routhier et al., 2021; Siedlinski et al., 2013.

claim: nAchR signaling is critical to maintain homeostasis not only in the context of oxidative stress, but under homeostatic conditions.
source: It is critical to note that the epithelial dysfunction observed in these animals, as well as part of the association of COPD risk with specific CHRNA loci, emerges independently of cigarette smoke (Parker et al., 2019; Routhier et al., 2021; Siedlinski et al., 2013), indicating that nAchR signaling is critical to maintain homeostasis not only in the context of oxidative stress, but under homeostatic conditions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that epithelial dysfunction occurs independently of cigarette smoke.

claim: Knockdown of nAchR subunits in fly ECs results in epithelial stress signaling in the absence of Paraquat exposure.
source: Supporting this view, our data show that knockdown of nAchR subunits in fly ECs also results in epithelial stress signaling in the absence of Paraquat exposure.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Disruption of 17 genes (~52%) resulted in enhancement of barrier dysfunction.
source: We found that disruption of 17 genes (~52%) resulted in enhancement (e.g. these genes were necessary for barrier integrity), while disruption of 4 genes (12%) resulted in suppression of the barrier dysfunction.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the screen results.

claim: Disruption of 4 genes (12%) resulted in suppression of the barrier dysfunction.
source: We found that disruption of 17 genes (~52%) resulted in enhancement (e.g. these genes were necessary for barrier integrity), while disruption of 4 genes (12%) resulted in suppression of the barrier dysfunction.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the screen results.

claim: Out of the 16 Drosophila hits where eQTL data was available for the corresponding human gene, 9 were consistent with the direction of the effect inferred from the association of the COPD risk allele with gene expression (56%).
source: Out of the 16 of Drosophila hits where eQTL data was available for the corresponding human gene, 9 were consistent with the direction of the effect inferred from the association of the COPD risk allele with gene expression (56%, Figure 1A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding comparing the screen results with human eQTL data, shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 2.
